_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- Texas rule seed, 2026-08-24. Loaded through add_rule.
Every rule below was read VERBATIM from the Texas Judicial Branch's own published
rule books at txcourts.gov: the Texas Rules of Civil Procedure and the Texas Rules
of Appellate Procedure (the latter printing 'Updated with Amendments Effective
January 1, 2026' on its first page). Rule 4 was additionally cross-checked against
the separate efiletexas.gov printing and the two agree word for word.
TWO COMPUTATION STANDARDS, AND UNLIKE CALIFORNIA THEY DISAGREE ON THE ARITHMETIC:
tx_trcp_4   Tex. R. Civ. P. 4      -- HAS a short-period exclusion
tx_trap_41  Tex. R. App. P. 4.1(a) -- has NONE
California's two standards produce the same dates and are kept apart so the audit
trail cites the authority that actually governs. Texas's two produce DIFFERENT
dates. A single blanket 'Texas' standard would be wrong on the numbers, not merely
on the citation. Each rule was read end to end; neither was inferred from the other,
and the fact that both live in the same state is not evidence they agree.
THE SHORT-PERIOD THRESHOLD IS THE THIRD ONE THIS ENGINE HAS HAD TO READ RATHER THAN
CARRY ACROSS, AND THE FIRST WHERE THE RULE'S NUMBER IS NOT THE FIELD'S NUMBER.
Ohio, Indiana and Florida all say 'less than seven days' and all carry 7. Texas says
'five days or less', which is <= 5, which is < 6 -- so tx_trcp_4 carries SIX. The
engine compares with a strict less-than. See the standard's own comment in
deadline-engine.js before touching that number. No Texas rule seeded here has a base
period of five days or less (the shortest is 20), so the property is currently
unreachable by construction and is kept anyway, because it is a property of Rule 4
rather than of the rows that happen to exist today.
THE ANSWER DEADLINE IS NOT A DAY COUNT AND THIS IS THE BIGGEST SINGLE THING ABOUT
TEXAS. Rule 99(b) does not give the defendant twenty days. It gives them until
'10:00 a.m. on the Monday next after the expiration of twenty days after the date of
service'. Three consequences, each of which is a way to get it wrong:
1. The deadline is always a MONDAY, from any weekday. Counting 20 days and rolling
off a weekend -- which is what every other jurisdiction in this engine does --
gives a date up to six days EARLY. A new terminal_day_rule mechanism was added
to the engine for this; rollover cannot express it.
2. 'Next after' is STRICT. When the twentieth day is itself a Monday the deadline
is the Monday of the FOLLOWING WEEK, because the twenty days expire at the end
of that Monday and the Monday next after an expiration cannot be the day the
expiration happened.
3. IT IS 10:00 A.M., NOT THE END OF THE DAY. This engine computes DATES. The
Texas answer deadline is an hour on that date, and a filing at 10:15 a.m. is
late. The rule row carries that warning in its note and the engine repeats it in
the audit trail, because a date alone understates this deadline by most of a
working day and default judgments have been taken on the difference.
THE EXPIRATION DAY IS NOT ROLLED BEFORE THE MONDAY IS FOUND. Proctor v. Green,
673 S.W.2d 390 (Tex. App.-Houston [1st Dist.] 1984), is reported as computing a
twentieth day of Sunday 3 July 1983, taking the Monday next after as 4 July 1983 --
the very next day -- and only then applying Rule 4 to move it off the holiday to
Tuesday 5 July. Rolling day twenty off the Sunday first would have produced 11 July.
The order is therefore fixed: count, find the Monday strictly after, then roll.
PROVENANCE OF THAT CASE, STATED PLAINLY. CourtListener confirms the case, court,
docket number, date and citation, but serves no accessible full text, and the two
databases that carry the opinion refused automated access. The holding and the
worked dates above come from a legal database's rendering of the opinion, NOT from a
primary source this session read directly. Nothing here rests on it: the same result
follows from Rule 99(b)'s own words, and the rule row cites Rule 99(b) as its
authority rather than the case. It is recorded because a reviewer should be able to
see exactly how far the verification went.
SERVICE EXTENSION: THREE DAYS, MAIL ONLY, AND NOT ON THE CITATION.
Rule 21a(c) adds three days for service by mail. Not for commercial delivery service,
not for fax, not for e-mail, and not for electronic service through the filing
manager -- 21a(b) gives each of those its own completion rule, and reading that list
as the set that qualifies under (c) would add three days Texas law does not add.
And 21a(a) covers every paper served under Rule 21 'other than the citation to be
served upon the filing of a cause of action', so the Rule 99 answer row carries NO
service extension. That is the law, not an omission.
Rule 4 expressly carves the Rule 21/21a three-day periods out of its own short-period
exclusion, so those three days count Saturdays, Sundays and holidays even though
three is under the threshold. The engine already behaves that way structurally --
verified at both call sites rather than assumed.
THE 50-DAY DISCOVERY CARVE-OUT IS FAMILY CODE ONLY IN THE CURRENT TEXT, AND OLDER
SOURCES SAY OTHERWISE. Rules 196.2(a), 197.2(a) and 198.2(a) each except 'a defendant
IN A SUIT GOVERNED BY THE FAMILY CODE served with a request before the defendant's
answer is due', who gets 50 days. The pre-2021 text of these rules said simply 'a
defendant', with no Family Code limit, and secondary sources reproducing that older
wording are still in circulation -- one was encountered while verifying this seed. In
ordinary civil litigation the 50-day alternative therefore does NOT apply under the
current rules, and no 50-day rows are seeded in the civil-litigation domain. Family
law is not a domain this engine covers.
EFFECTIVE DATES, AND A REAL MISMATCH WITH HOW THIS ENGINE SELECTS RULES.
The civil rows carry effective_from 2021-01-01, from the Supreme Court of Texas's own
order, Misc. Docket No. 20-9153 (dated December 23, 2020), which gave final approval
'effective January 1, 2021'. Every civil rule seeded here is one that order amended.
But that order keys applicability to the date the CASE WAS FILED, not to the date the
period runs from: 'The amendments apply to cases filed on or after January 1, 2021 ...
The rules amended by this Order continue to govern procedures and limitations in cases
filed before January 1, 2021.' This engine selects a rule version by the date the
period runs from, and has no field for when the case was filed. So for a case filed in
late 2020 whose service or discovery happened in 2021, these rows are the WRONG
version and the engine cannot tell. Disclosed rather than papered over; a matter
opened before 2021 needs the pre-2021 text checked by hand.
A Texas matter whose period runs from before 2021-01-01 is REFUSED rather than
computed. The pre-2021 text was not read verbatim here -- the same call already made
for Pennsylvania's pre-2024 matters and Florida's pre-edition matters. To extend
backwards, read the earlier text and add a superseding row; never widen these by
assumption.
The appellate rows carry effective_from 2026-01-01, the amendment date printed on the
edition actually read. Rule 26.1's own text is materially older, but the rule book
prints no per-rule amendment history, so this follows the Florida convention of using
the edition date rather than inventing a history.
THE FOUR APPELLATE PERIODS ARE FOUR SEPARATE ROWS WITH FOUR DIFFERENT TRIGGER NAMES,
not one rule with variants. All four run from the same real-world event -- the
judgment being signed -- but which period applies is a case fact (was a qualifying
post-judgment motion filed, is this an accelerated appeal, is this a restricted
appeal). The engine has no field for any of those, so it must never choose between
them; distinct trigger names force the caller to say which situation they are in.
Same treatment as Florida's 45-day defendant alternatives, Michigan's in-state versus
out-of-state service rows and California's unlawful detainer variants.
NOT ENCODED, deliberately, and flagged rather than dropped:
1. Tex. R. App. P. 26.1(d): 'if any party timely files a notice of appeal, another
party may file a notice of appeal within the applicable period stated above or 14
days after the first filed notice of appeal, whichever is later.' One limb is a
period this engine itself computed rather than an event date, so its 'later of'
cannot be expressed by the multi-trigger shape, which resolves between supplied
DATES. Same class as Ohio App.R. 4(B)(1) cross-appeal and FRCP 15(a)(3). Named,
not improvised.
2. Tex. R. App. P. 4.1(b), the clerk's-office-closed limb -- an appellate filing
period extends when the clerk's office is closed or inaccessible on the last day.
Unknowable in advance. Same class as Indiana's office-closed limb, Illinois's
Governor-proclamation limb, Florida's chief-justice hurricane limb and
California's CCP 12b. Tex. R. Civ. P. 4 has NO such limb -- verified by reading it
in full, because a widely repeated secondary claim says otherwise.
3. Tex. R. App. P. 4.2 and 4.3, which move or restart appellate periods when a party
received no notice of the judgment, or when the judgment is modified. Both are
real and citable; 4.2 requires a trial court finding of the date notice was
received, which is an event this engine would need supplied and a shape closer to
trigger substitution than to anything seeded here. Left for a later phase rather
than approximated.
4. Tex. R. App. P. 26.3, extension of time to file the notice of appeal. A motion,
granted or not by the court; the engine cannot see one.
5. Tex. R. Civ. P. 5's general enlargement power, and every 'unless a different time
is set by the parties' agreement or court order' clause in Rule 194.2(a), and the
court-order escapes throughout the discovery rules. A court order or a Rule 11
agreement displaces these dates and the engine cannot see either.
6. Tex. R. Civ. P. 190's discovery-control-plan deadlines and the requirement that a
discovery request be served no later than 30 days before the end of the discovery
period. That end date is set per case by the control plan or by court order, not
by a rule, so there is no fixed period to compute from.
7. The Rule 99 answer deadline's TIME of day. See point 3 in the answer-deadline note
above -- this is a disclosure, not a silent truncation.
8. Every criminal limb: Tex. R. App. P. 26.2, and Rule 99's application in suits
governed by the Family Code. Outside this engine's domains.

rules.label: Answer to a petition after service of citation (Texas)

authority.quote: The citation shall direct the defendant to file a written answer to the plaintiff's petition on or before 10:00 a.m. on the Monday next after the expiration of twenty days after the date of service thereof.
authority.note: THE SINGLE MOST MISCOMPUTED DEADLINE IN THIS ENGINE, and the only one whose shape no other jurisdiction shares. It is NOT a twenty-day period. The twenty days only fix a point after which the deadline lands on the next MONDAY, and 'next after' is strict -- a twentieth day falling on a Monday moves the deadline a full week, not to that same day. IT IS ALSO 10:00 A.M., NOT MIDNIGHT. This engine computes dates; the real deadline is that hour on the date returned, and a filing later that day is late enough to support a default judgment. Treat the returned date as the morning of, never the end of. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, by law rather than by omission: Rule 21a(a) covers papers served under Rule 21 'other than the citation to be served upon the filing of a cause of action', so the 21a(c) three days for mail do not reach this deadline. NOT encoded: Rule 99's application in Family Code suits, and Rule 5's general enlargement power. effective_from is 2021-01-01 per Misc. Docket No. 20-9153; note that order keys applicability to the date the CASE WAS FILED, which this engine cannot see -- see the file readme.

rules.label: Initial disclosures, measured from the first answer or general appearance (Texas)

authority.quote: A party must make the initial disclosures within 30 days after the filing of the first answer or general appearance unless a different time is set by the parties' agreement or court order.
authority.note: TEXAS REQUIRES INITIAL DISCLOSURES WITHOUT ANY REQUEST, which is why this row exists at all -- there is no discovery request to serve, and nothing for a practitioner to receive as a prompt. Rule 194.1(a) makes it a standing duty: a party must provide the Rule 194.2 material 'without awaiting a discovery request'. Rule 99(c)'s citation notice now warns the defendant of it in terms. This is the FIRST-ANSWER limb; the same subdivision carries a second limb for a party joined later, which runs from a different event and is its own row (tx-trcp-1942a-initial-disclosures-later-joined). NO SERVICE EXTENSION: Rule 21a(c) adds days after SERVICE of a paper, and this clock starts on the FILING of an answer, not on service of anything. The 'unless a different time is set by the parties' agreement or court order' clause is a real escape the engine cannot see. NOT encoded: Rule 194.2(c)'s exemptions and the Family Code carve-out in Rule 194.1(a).

rules.label: Initial disclosures for a party served or joined after the first answer (Texas)

authority.quote: A party that is first served or otherwise joined after the filing of the first answer or general appearance must make the initial disclosures within 30 days after being served or joined, unless a different time is set by the parties' agreement or court order.
authority.note: A DIFFERENT CLOCK FROM A DIFFERENT EVENT, which is why it is its own row rather than a variant of the first-answer one -- the same treatment given Florida's 45-day defendant alternatives and Michigan's in-state versus out-of-state service rows. Which limb applies is a case fact (was this party in the suit when the first answer was filed), and the engine has no field for it and does not choose. NO SERVICE EXTENSION attached even though this limb does mention being served: Rule 21a(a) reaches papers served under Rule 21, not service of process bringing a new party into the suit, and Rule 21a(c) adds time after service of 'a notice or other paper'. Reading the word 'served' here as triggering 21a(c) would add three days on a shape 21a does not govern.

authority.quote: The responding party must serve a written response on the requesting party within 30 days after service of the interrogatories, except that a defendant in a suit governed by the Family Code served with a request before the defendant's answer is due need not respond until 50 days after service of the request.
authority.note: A REAL RESPONSE DEADLINE, unlike Ohio's and Indiana's interrogatory rules, which set only a floor on a period the requesting party designates. Texas fixes the window directly, so the date this produces is a genuine due date. The 50-day alternative in the quoted text is FAMILY CODE ONLY under the current rule and is not seeded -- the pre-2021 text said simply 'a defendant', and secondary sources still reproduce that older wording; see the file readme. Service extension is three days for MAIL ONLY under Rule 21a(c) -- not fax, e-mail, commercial delivery or electronic service through the filing manager.

rules.label: Written response to a request for production and inspection (Texas)

authority.quote: The responding party must serve a written response on the requesting party within 30 days after service of the request, except that a defendant in a suit governed by the Family Code served with a request before the defendant's answer is due need not respond until 50 days after service of the request.
authority.note: Like Florida's Rule 1.350(b)(3) and unlike Illinois's Rule 214(a) and Ohio's Civ.R. 34(B), this is a real RESPONSE deadline rather than a minimum period the requesting party must allow. The date produced is a due date, not a floor. NOT encoded from the same rule: Rule 196.1(a)'s requirement that the request itself be served no later than 30 days before the end of the discovery period -- that end date is fixed per case by the discovery control plan or a court order, not by any rule, so there is no period to compute from. The 50-day alternative is Family Code only; see the file readme.

rules.label: Response to requests for admissions before the matter is admitted (Texas)

authority.quote: The responding party must serve a written response on the requesting party within 30 days after service of the request ... If a response is not timely served, the request is considered admitted without the necessity of a court order.
authority.note: SELF-EXECUTING, WHICH MAKES IT THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL DEADLINE IN THE TEXAS CIVIL SET. Rule 198.2(c) admits the matter by operation of the rule on a missed response -- no motion and no order, the same shape as Ill. S. Ct. R. 216(c) and Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.370(a)(6), and expressly NOT the shape California uses, where the deemed-admitted consequence runs through a separate motion under CCP 2033.280. Rule 198.3 then makes an admission 'conclusively established' unless the court permits withdrawal or amendment on the two findings it names. Both subdivisions are quoted together above because the timing sentence alone understates what missing this date costs. The 50-day alternative is Family Code only; see the file readme.

rules.label: Notice of appeal in a civil case, ordinary 30-day period (Texas)

authority.quote: The notice of appeal must be filed within 30 days after the judgment is signed, except as follows:
authority.note: THE TRIGGER IS THE SIGNING OF THE JUDGMENT, not its entry, not its rendition and not service of notice of it. Texas differs here from California, whose Rule 8.104 limbs run from service of a notice of entry, and from Florida, whose trigger is rendition. A user who supplies an entry or service date to this row gets a wrong answer. THIS IS THE DEFAULT PERIOD AND THREE THINGS DISPLACE IT, each its own row: a timely post-judgment motion (90 days), an accelerated appeal (20 days), a restricted appeal (six months). Which applies is a case fact the engine has no field for, so it never chooses -- check all four before relying on this one. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: this period runs from an act of the court rather than from service of a paper, and Tex. R. App. P. 9.5's service provisions were not read for this seed, so none is attached rather than one being assumed. NOT encoded: 26.1(d)'s cross-appeal limb, 26.3's extension motion, and 4.2/4.3. See the file readme.

rules.label: Notice of appeal in a civil case where a qualifying post-judgment motion was timely filed, 90 days (Texas)

authority.quote: the notice of appeal must be filed within 90 days after the judgment is signed if any party timely files: (1) a motion for new trial; (2) a motion to modify the judgment; (3) a motion to reinstate under Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 165a; or (4) a request for findings of fact and conclusions of law if findings and conclusions either are required by the Rules of Civil Procedure or, if not required, could properly be considered by the appellate court
authority.note: STILL COUNTED FROM THE SIGNING OF THE JUDGMENT, NOT FROM THE MOTION OR ITS DISPOSITION. This is the trap in this row and it runs the opposite way from the federal analogue: FRAP 4(a)(4)(A) makes a qualifying post-judgment motion REPLACE the trigger, so the federal clock restarts from the order disposing of the motion. Texas does not restart anything -- it lengthens the same period, still measured from the day the judgment was signed. Routing this through the engine's trigger-substitution shape, which exists for the federal rule, would produce a date months late. It is a separate row rather than a retrigger clause for exactly that reason. Note also that the condition is a motion TIMELY FILED BY ANY PARTY, not by the appellant, and that limb (4) turns on whether findings could properly be considered -- both are case facts the engine cannot see, which is why the caller must select this trigger deliberately.

rules.label: Notice of appeal in an accelerated appeal, 20 days (Texas)

authority.quote: in an accelerated appeal, the notice of appeal must be filed within 20 days after the judgment or order is signed;
authority.note: TWENTY DAYS, TEN FEWER THAN THE DEFAULT, and this is where the two Texas computation standards diverging actually bites. Tex. R. Civ. P. 4 excludes weekends and holidays from periods of five days or less; Tex. R. App. P. 4.1 has no such exclusion at all. Twenty days is over the civil threshold anyway, but the point stands for anything shorter in this domain: nothing in the appellate rules excludes intermediate weekends, and applying the civil rule's exclusion here would push an appellate deadline LATER than the true one. Whether an appeal is accelerated is fixed by statute or by Rule 28 for the case type, not by anything this engine can see, so it never selects this row for the caller. Alongside Michigan's 21-day period and Pennsylvania's 10-day subject-matter periods, this is another reason a thirty-day appeal habit does not survive a state line.

rules.label: Notice of appeal in a restricted appeal, six months (Texas)

authority.quote: in a restricted appeal, the notice of appeal must be filed within six months after the judgment or order is signed; and
authority.note: SIX MONTHS, NOT 180 DAYS, and the rule says months so the row does. The engine counts months by anniversary date with end-of-month clamping, so a judgment signed 31 August yields 28 or 29 February rather than 2 or 3 March. Encoding this as 180 days would be a different date in most months and would misquote a rule that chose the word 'months'. Contrast California's Rule 8.104(a)(1)(C), which really does say 180 days and is encoded that way -- the two look interchangeable and are not. A restricted appeal is available only to a party who did not participate in the hearing and did not timely file a post-judgment motion, request for findings or notice of appeal (Tex. R. App. P. 30); that is a case fact the engine has no field for and never infers.

rules.label: Notice of appeal by another party after a first-filed notice, ordinary 30-day appeal only, the later of that period and 14 days (Texas)

limbs.label: 30 days after the judgment is signed, the ordinary Rule 26.1 period
14 days after the first notice of appeal was filed

authority.quote: if any party timely files a notice of appeal, another party may file a notice of appeal within the applicable period stated above or 14 days after the first filed notice of appeal, whichever is later.
authority.note: NOW COMPUTABLE, BUT ONLY FOR THE ORDINARY APPEAL, AND THE RULE ID SAYS SO. Refused by this engine until 2026-08-24 because the limbs carry different counts (30 and 14) from different events. THE CATCH THAT MAKES TEXAS HARDER THAN OHIO OR NEW YORK: limb one is "the applicable period stated above", and Rule 26.1 states FOUR of them -- 30 days ordinarily, 90 where a qualifying post-judgment motion was filed, 20 in an accelerated appeal, and six months in a restricted appeal. Which applies is a case fact the engine has no field for. This row encodes the 30-day ordinary period ONLY. NO ROW IS SEEDED for a cross-appeal off an accelerated, post-judgment-motion-extended or restricted appeal, and that is an explicit decision: each would need its own trigger vocabulary, and guessing between four periods is exactly what this engine must not do. If the underlying appeal is anything other than an ordinary 30-day appeal, DO NOT use this row -- compute limb one from the correct Rule 26.1 variant and take the later by hand. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: neither limb runs from service of a paper on a party, and Tex. R. App. P. 9.5 was not read for this seed.
